title: 63-203 Excluded Resources
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Excluded Resources Number Page 63-203 1 of 4 Revision Date: 09/01/2026 B ackground: CalFresh households (HHs) who are not Categorical ly Eligible (CE) or Modified Categorical ly Eligible (MCE) must not exceed the maximum allowable non- exempt property limit as detailed in Section 63- 1101. This section was revised due to sunset review, there are no federal or state legislative changes. P olicy: Exclude the following resources when determining the HH’s eligibility to CalFresh when not CE or MCE. 1. R eal Property Exclude the following categories of real property from resource consideration: • The home and surrounding property as long as the land is not separated from the home by property owned by someone else. Public roads or rights of way that run through the property do not affect the exemption of the property. The home and surrounding property remain exempt if they are temporarily unoccupied for reasons of employment, training for future employment, illness, or uninhabitability caused by natural disaster, if the HH intends to return. • Property that produces income each year that is equal to its fair market value. This includes property used seasonally, such as rental or vacation homes. Refer to Processing Guide 200-01 to determine whether the property is producing income. • Indian lands held jointly with the Tribe or lands that can only be sold with the approval of the Department of the Interior’s Bureau of Indian Affairs. • The portion of real property needed to maintain or use an excluded vehicle is not counted as a resource. Example Scenario A HH owns a produce truck to earn income but cannot park it in a residential area. Instead, they use a quarter-acre of their 100-acre field to park and service the truck. Outcome Exclude the value of the quarter-acre only, not the value of the entire field. 2. HH Goods, Personal Effects, and Pension Plans Exclude HH goods and personal effects including: • One burial plot per HH member. • The cash value of one funeral agreement per HH member, provided that the agreement does not exceed $1,500 in equity value. Any amount above $1,500 will be counted in the resource amount. • The cash value of life insurance policies. F or types of retirement savings and pension plans that are excluded from consideration as resources refer to the Excluded Retirement Savings and Pension Plans Desk Aid. 3. Vehicles Exclude all vehicles as a resource. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Excluded Resources Number Page 63-203 2 of 4 4. Resources with Equity Value of $1,500 or Less Resources with an equity value of $1,500 or less, excluding financial instruments such as stocks, bonds, and negotiable financial instruments. 5. Property Essential to Employment Exclude property that is essential to the employment or self-employment of a HH member such as: • Farmland, work-related equipment, tools or machinery. • Business resources, such as funds in a checking or savings account, as long as the funds represent averaged self-employment income or the funds needed to produce that income, for the period of time used in the average. N ote: When a HH member ceases to be self-employed in farming, property which was essential to this self-employment will continue to be excluded as a resource for a period of one year from the date of termination. 6. Installment Contracts, Notes Receivable and Trust Deeds Exclude the following as resources: • Installment contracts for the sale of land or buildings if they produce income equal to their fair market value. The same rule applies to the value of the property being sold under the contract or used as security for the sale. • Notes receivable and trust deeds if the HH receives income from the trust deed or note receivable that matches their fair market value. 7. Individual Development Accounts (IDA) Exclude funds in a Temporary Assistance for Needy Families (TANF) IDA as a resource for any period in which the HH member keeps or adds funds into the account. 8 . Disaster Loans & Grants Exclude governmental payments designated for the restoration of a home damaged in a disaster. This includes payments from the Department of Housing and Urban Development, disaster loans, or grants made by the Small Business Administration. 9. Inaccessible Resources Exclude resources that have a cash value, however are not accessible to the HH. These resources include, but are not limited to: • Security deposits on rental property or utilities. • Property in probate. • Real property which the HH is making a good faith effort to sell at a reasonable price, and which has not yet been sold. • Nutritional Assistance Program (NAP) benefits issued in the United States territories of Puerto Rico, American Samoa, and the Commonwealth of the Northern Marianas. These benefits are not accessible once the HH member is in the United States. • Property, other than financial instruments ( for example, stocks, bonds, and legally binding promissory notes) which if sold or otherwise disposed would produce more than $1,500. • Irrevocable trust funds. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Excluded Resources Number Page 63-203 3 of 4 Funds in, or moved into a trust , and any income it earns, will be considered inaccessible to the HH if all of the following are true: • The trustee is a court, an institution, corporation, or organization not controlled by a HH member, or is court-appointed with court-imposed limits on how the funds can be used. • The funds held in irrevocable trust are established with the HH’s own funds as long as the trustee only uses the funds for investments or to pay educational or medical expenses for someone named by the trust, or established by non-HH funds by a non-HH member. • The trust does not invest in or support a business controlled by a HH member. • The trust is expected to continue through the certification period. • No HH member has the power to revoke the trust arrangement or change the name of the beneficiary during the certification period. N ote: If information is questionable, verification will be obtained through a collateral contact or documentation. 1 0. Funds Prorated as Income Exclude resources of students or self-employed HH members that have been prorated as income. This exclusion also applies to the funds of ineligible non- citizens or disqualified HH members whose resources are considered available to the HH. 1 1. Federal Tax Credits and Refunds - Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) Exclude federal tax refunds including but not limited to, over-withheld income tax, EITC, and Child Tax Credit (CTC) for 12 calendar months after the refund is received. 1 2. Lien Placed on Non-Liquid Resources Exclude a non-liquid asset if a lien has been placed as a result of taking out a business loan, and the HH is prohibited by the security or lien agreement with the lien holder (creditor) from selling the asset. 1 3. Resources of Individuals Receiving Public Assistance (PA) Exclude the r esources of HH members receiving PA. If a resource is jointly held by a CalFresh HH member who is receiving PA and a CalFresh HH member who is not receiving PA, the amount counted in determining the PA eligibility will be excluded. 1 4. Restricted Accounts CalFresh recipients (not applicants) will be allowed to retain unlimited cash reserves in one or more restricted accounts at a financial institution. These funds are in addition to the existing resource limits currently allowed. To be excluded as a resource, the funds must be retained for one or more of the following specific purposes: • Purchase of a home. • Education or training. • Start-up of a new business. T he HH must establish and maintain a restricted account separately from any other accounts. Refer to Processing Guide 200-01 for information on the treatment of Restricted Accounts.

title: 63-222 Earned Income
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number Page Earned Income 63-222 1 of 2 Revision Date: 07/01/2022 Background: Federal law requires earned income to be included in the eligibility determination for CalFresh. Purpose: This section defines earned income which must be included in the budget calculation. The section is being revised to merge information regarding military pay. Policy: Earned income is any monetary compensation received for the performance of work. Earned income shall include but is not limited to: Type Information Diverted Wages Wages earned by a household (HH) member that are garnished or diverted by an employer and paid to a third party for a HH’s expenses such as rent. Federal and State Work Study Income Any remaining amount of federal and state work study which has not been excluded per Section 63-224. In Home Supportive Services (IHSS) IHSS wages, even if the services are being provided to a HH member. Military Pay Military personnel are paid semi-monthly; however, they only receive one check stub each month which shows the total gross and net income for the entire month. Military pay includes special allowances showing in the “Entitlement” (ENT) section of the “Leave and Earnings Statement” (LES). Special allowances include but are not limited to the following: •Basic Allowance for Housing (BAH) •Basic Allowance for Subsistence (BAS) •Family Separation Allowance (FSA) •Variable Housing Allowance (VHA) Refer to Section 63-224 for a list of excluded military special allowance and to Desk Aid Military Pay LES for more info. Pay Advances Advances on wages, when reasonably anticipated, will be counted in the month received. Salaries Monetary compensation quoted to and paid to an employee on an annual basis. Self-Employment Refer to Section 63-225 for more information. Severance Payments Reoccurring severance payments received. Refer to Section 63-224 for treatment of lump sum payments. Striker’s benefits Any portion of striker’s benefits received as compensation for picketing. Title I Volunteers in Service to America (VISTA) Program Stipends An AmeriCorps VISTA stipend received by an applicant must be counted. Refer to Section 63-224 for the treatment of VISTA stipends when a CalFresh recipient joins the VISTA program while on aid. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number Page Earned Income 63-222 2 of 2 Training Allowances Training allowances from vocational and rehabilitation programs recognized by federal, state, or local governments, to the extent they are not a reimbursement. Wages Monetary compensation paid to an employee based on the number of hours worked. Wages Held by an Employer Wages held at the request of the employee in the month the wages would have been paid by the employer. Refer to Section 63-224 for treatment of wages involuntarily held by the employer. Wages or Salary Paid to the Owner of a Closely Held Corporation An owner/shareholder who works and receives a salary or wages from the corporation is not a self-employed individual; he or she is an employee. Workforce Investment Act (WIA) On-the-Job- Training Earnings Earnings of individuals who are participating in on-the-job training programs under Section 204(b)(1)(C) or Section 264(c)(1)(A) of the WIA, or under Title I of the National and Community Services Act (NCSA) of 1990, except as specified in Section 63-224. NCSA includes but is not limited to the following programs: Serve America, American Conservation and Youth Corps, and National and Community Service subtitles. References: CFR 273.9(b)(1), MPP 63-502, ACIN I-79-03, I-79-03 EII, I-84-09(e), I-34-17. Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance on or by 07/31/2025 Approval for Release: Rick Wanne, Director Self Sufficiency Services

title: 63-223 Unearned Income
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageUnearned Income 63-223 1 of 3 Revision Date: 07/01/2022 Background: Unearned income is any income coming from a gain or benefit and not classified as earned or excluded income. Purpose: The purpose of this section is to define unearned income which must be included in the CalFresh (CF) budget calculation. This section is being revised to include the treatment of cryptocurrency for CF. Policy: Unearned income detailed below must be counted in the CF budget calculation. Income, which is garnished for a household (HH) expense, will be counted. CalWORKs (CW) and General Relief (GR) grants or other public assistance programs reduced due to failure to comply will be counted. Type Description Assistance Payments CW, GR, Refugee Cash Assistance, or other public assistance programs. Adoption Assistance Program (AAP) Support payments provided to adoptive parents. Any portion of the adoption payment that is earmarked for reimbursement will be excluded. Refer to CFPG 63-224 for a list of allowable exclusions. Annuities A form of insurance or investment entitling the investor to a series of annual sums. Child Support or Alimony Support payments for children or spouses made directly to the HH from non HH members or received directly from the Local Child Support Agency. Include the child support disregard applied to CWs recipients. Refer to CFPG 63-224 for additional child support exclusion guidance. Cryptocurrency A digital or virtual currency. Cryptocurrency is a countable non-liquid resource. If the cryptocurrency is… then it is considered… a one-time conversion, a non-recurring lump sum payment and excluded as income. Refer to 63-224. converted to cash on a recurring basis, unearned income. Deemed Income Income received from a sponsor paid to a sponsored noncitizen. Refer to CFPG 63- 157 and 63-246 for additional information. Disability Insurance Benefits Privately purchased disability insurance benefits received by the HH. Employment Development Department (EDD) Benefits Unemployment Insurance Benefits (UIB), State Disability Insurance (SDI), California Training Benefits (CTB), or Paid Family Leave (PFL). Refer to CFPG 63-224 and the UIB-SDI Reductions Determination Table for UIB deductions or offsets. Foster Care Payments or Approved Relative Care (ARC) Support payment received for the care of foster youth, including Non-Minor Dependent (NMD). This includes ARC payments paid to relatives approved to care for minor relatives. Refer to CFPG 63-224 for income exclusions. Gift Cards Reasonably anticipated prepaid gift cards such as American Express, MasterCard, or Visa. Establishment-specific gift cards are excluded as income and resources. Lottery Winnings HH winnings in which payments are received in lump sum or installments. Refer to CFPG 63-283 for additional information on lottery winnings. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageUnearned Income 63-223 2 of 3 Payments Considered Gain or Benefit All other direct money payment from any source, which can be construed to be a gain or benefit. This includes payments from government-sponsored programs, dividends, interest, and royalties. Pension or Retirement Benefits Regularly paid benefits received from an employer to an employee in retirement. Refugee Benefits Reception and Placement (R&P) Income/Resettlement Agency (RA) also known as Voluntary Agency (VOLAG) funds may be considered unearned income depending on how they are disbursed or who provides them. Refer to CFPG 63-224 for a detailed listing of allowable exclusions. Reimbursements Reimbursements that exceed total expenses or which are intended to cover living expenses, such as food, rent, and clothing. Refer to CFPG 63-224 for a list of excluded reimbursements. Resident Opportunity and Self Sufficiency (ROSS) Grants A program for public housing residents that provides supportive payments for participating in resident activities that assist in becoming economically self-sufficient. Social Security Benefits Supplemental Security Income/State Supplementary Payment (SSI/SSP) including retirement, disability, survivors, and supplemental benefits received from the Social Security Administration (SSA). Strikers’ Benefits Benefits provided to workers on strike, the portion received as compensation for picketing is earned income. Trust Income Income and dividends withdrawn from a trust, will be counted in the month they become available to the HH. Veterans Benefits Veteran/Survivors Pension, Aid and Attendance (AA) benefits, and Educational Assistance received from the Veterans’ Administration (VA). Note: Educational Assistance must be prorated over the period the benefit is expected to cover and educational expenses must be excluded. Refer to CFPG 63- 224 for allowable exclusions. Worker’s Compensation Wage compensation benefits provided by the employer in the event of an injury. Rental Income Income derived from rental property in which a HH member is not actively engaged in the management of the property at least an average of 20 hours a week. Refer to CFPG 63-222 for guidance when the HH is engaged in the property management. Educational Assistance Non-excluded scholarships, educational grants, or fellowships. Refer to CFPG 63- 224 for a list of excluded educational assistance. Note: Educational Assistance must be prorated over the period the benefit is expected to cover and educational expenses must be excluded. Refer to CFPG 63- 224 for allowable exclusions. References: ACL 21-137, ACIN I-68-17, I-58-08, I-18-07, I-52-06, I-91-06, I-16-05, I-34-04 State Policy Interpretation # 21-45 Cryptocurrency Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance on or by 07/31/2025. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageUnearned Income 63-223 3 of 3 Approval for Release: Rick Wanne, Director Self-Sufficiency Services

title: 63-224 Income Exclusions
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 1 of 10 Revision Date: 05/01/2022 Background: Excluded income is any income that will not count in the CalFresh budget when determining eligibility. Purpose: The purpose of this section clarifies income that will not be counted when determining eligibility. This section is being revised to align with recent state policy changes. Effective December 1, 2021, student loans and grants excluded for CalWORKs must also be excluded for CalFresh. Policy: Excluded income detailed below must not be counted in the CalFresh budget calculation. Excluded income shall include but is not limited to: Type Description Agent Orange Settlement Fund Payments received from the Agent Orange Settlement Fund under the Agent Orange Compensation Act of 1989. Benefits Received by Children Special Supplemental Food Program for Women, Infants, and Children (WIC), Special Milk Program, School Breakfast and Lunch Programs, Summer Food Service Program for Children, Commodity Distribution Program, and Child/Adult Care Food Program. Board of Governors Grant (BOGG) Fee Waiver The amount of the BOGG fee waiver. California Victims of Crimes Payments received under the California Victims of Crimes Program. Cash Donations Cash donations received from one or more private, nonprofit charitable organizations of not more than $300 in a calendar quarter. Child Care Payments Made Under Title IV-A Any childcare payment made under Title IV-A of the Social Security Act, including transitional childcare and the Child Care and Development Block Grant. Child Support Transferred to the District Attorney Child support payments received by CalWORKs recipients, directly from a non-household member that must be transferred to the District Attorney’s office or other county agency, to maintain CalWORKs eligibility. Exclude the child support income when the customer assigns child support rights to the county (signs the Notice and Agreement for Child, Spousal and Medical Support [CW 2.1]). Contributions from People or Organizations Contributions as income when it is meant for a specific expenditure (for example, rent). Department of Allowances for training expenses paid to recipients participating in County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 2 of 10 Rehabilitation Training Allowances Department of Rehabilitation programs. Domestic Volunteer Services Act Any payment to volunteers under Title II of the Domestic Volunteer Services Act, including but not limited to the Retired Senior Volunteer Program (RSVP), Foster Grandparents Program and Senior Companion Program. Earnings of a Minor Child The earned income from a child, when they are elementary or secondary school students at least half time and have not attained their 18th birthday. •Exclude the earned income of a student turning 18 years of age during the certification period or initial application until the month following the month the student turns 18. The exclusion continues to apply during temporary interruptions in school attendance due to semester or vacation breaks, provided the child’s enrollment will resume following the break. If the child’s earnings or amount of work performed cannot be differentiated from that of other household (HH) members, prorate the total earnings equally among the working members and exclude child’s prorated share. •Individuals are considered children for purposes of this provision if they are under the parental control of another HH member. Note: The unearned income (For example, Social Security) of a child under 18 is not excluded. Educational Assistance In general, education assistance is considered excluded income when determining eligibility. Educational assistance, including grants, scholarships, fellowships, work study, educational loans on which payment is deferred, veterans' educational benefits and the like will be excluded. Refer to Educational Assistance Desk Aid. Exclude educational assistance not otherwise excluded by federal statute, to the extent that it is either earmarked by the lender, used for, or intended to be used for, allowable educational expenses at qualifying institutions. The following financial educational assistance is excluded: •Bureau of Indian Affairs student assistance programs. •Grants administered by the Federal Secretary of Education. •Loans or grants administered by: oCommunity college extended opportunity services. oCalifornia Student Aid Commission (CSAC). oA college accredited by the Western Association of Schools and Colleges. •Needs-based grants for undergraduate students. •Awards and scholarships for dependent children. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 3 of 10 •Grants not available to the student to meet current needs. •Any other loans which have a written agreement specifying to repay and a repayment plan. •Any other educational assistance when is used for allowable educational expenses. •Title XIII, Indian Higher Education Programs, Tribal Development Student Assistance Revolving Loan Program, and the Carl D. Perkins Vocational and Applied Technology Education Act Amendments of 1990. •A program funded in whole or part under Title IV of the Higher Education Act which include: oBasic Educational Opportunity Grants (BEOG). oDirect Graduate PLUS Loans. oDirect PLUS Loans. oDirect Subsidized/Unsubsidized Loans. oFederal Pell Grants. oFederal Perkins Loans. oFederal Stafford Loans. oGrants to States for Student Incentives. oGuaranteed Student Loan Program. oIraq and Afghanistan Service Grant. oSpecial Programs for Students from Disadvantaged Background. oSupplemental Educational Opportunity Grants (SEOG). oTeacher Education Assistance for College and Higher Education Grants (TEACH). oVeterans’ Educational Outreach Program. Verify all factors affecting educational assistance. The student is responsible for providing information to document the amounts claimed for tuition, mandatory fees, books, supplies, transportation, dependent care, and miscellaneous personal expenses. Any portion of assistance received that is not used for allowable expenses will not be excluded. Emergency Assistance under the Disaster Relief Act of 1974 Federal major disaster and emergency assistance provided under the Disaster Relief Act of 1974, and comparable assistance provided by states, local governments, and disaster assistance organizations. Employment and Training Payments Any payment made to a CalFresh Employment and Training (CFET) program participant for costs that are reasonably necessary and directly related to participation in the program. Excluded CFET payments for costs include, but are not limited to: •Dependent care costs. •Transportation. •Other costs related to work, training, or education, such as uniforms, personal safety items or other necessary equipment and books or County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 4 of 10 training manuals. Exception: The costs of meals. Federal and State Work Study Program Income received from any federal and state Work Study program that is allocated for educational expenses. Refer to Excluded Educational Assistance Desk Aid. Foster Care or Approved Relative Caretaker Program (ARC) Payments Foster care or ARC payments received by HHs with foster care children, who by the HH’s choice are excluded and not part of the CalFresh HH. When a child has returned to their home, do not include former foster care payments in the budget. Funds and payments to Native American Tribal members or Alaskan Natives Funds and payments received by the following: •Bad River Band of the Lake Superior Tribe of Chippewa Indians of Wisconsin. •Blackfeet Tribe. •Cherokee Nation of Oklahoma. •Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe. •Crow Creek Sioux Tribe. •Lower Brule Sioux Tribe. •Devils Lake Sioux Tribe. •Fort Belknap Indian Community. •Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes. •Lac Corte Oreilles Band of Lake Superior Chippewa Indians. •Keweenaw Bay Indian Community. •Minnesota Chippewa Tribe. •Navajo Tribe, Oglala Sioux Tribe. •Rosebud Sioux Tribe. •Shoshone-Bannock Tribe. •The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe. •Grand River Band of Ottawa Indians. •Confederated Tribes and Bands of the Yakima Indian Nation and the Apache Tribe of the Mescalero Reservation from the Indian Claims Commission. •Passamaquoddy Tribe, the Penobscot Nation, or the Houlton Band of Maliseet, or any Indian HH or member thereof, pursuant to the Main Indian Claims Settlement Act of 1980. •Relocation Assistance to members of the Navajo and Hopi Tribes. •Indian Claims Commission or Claims Court. •Interests of Individual Indians in Trusts. •Indian Child Welfare Act that has children or family services granted through a program on or near reservations. •Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Arizona. •Blackfeet, Gros Ventre, Assiniboine tribes, Montana, and the Papago, Red Lake Band of Chippewa Indians. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 5 of 10 •White Earth Band of Chippewa Indians, Minnesota, pursuant to the White Earth Reservation Land Settlement Act of 1985. •Saginaw Chippewa Indian Tribe of Michigan. •Members of the Assiniboine Tribe of the Fort Belknap Indian Community and the Fort Peck Indian Reservation Montana. •Heirs of deceased Native Americans under the Old Age Assistance Clams Act except for per capita shares exceeding $2,000. •Funds distributed per capita or held in trust for the Chippewas of Lake Superior and the Chippewas of the Mississippi. •Assets or income from the trust fund established to the Puyallup Tribe of Indians Settlement Act of 1989. •Payments made to the Seminole Nation of Oklahoma, the Seminole Tribe of Florida, the Miccosukee Tribe of Indians of Florida, and the independent Seminole Indians of Florida to satisfy the judgements of the Indians Claims Commission, except as per capita payments exceeding $2,000. •Payments, funds distributions or income under the Seneca Nation Settlement Act of 1990. Garnished and Diverted Wages •Income received as a vendor payment if an employer pays a HH rent directly to the landlord in addition to paying regular wages. •Earned in-kind if an employer provides housing in addition to wages. •Count as income wages earned by a HH member that are garnished or diverted by an employer and paid to a third party for a HH’s expenses such as rent. General Relief General Relief vendor payment is not counted as income to the HH, except when the payment is for housing or energy assistance. Independent Living Program (ILP) Income and incentive payments earned by children 16 years of age or older participating in the ILP when received as part of the ILP written transitional independent living plan. There is no limit to the amount exempted under this subsection. Infrequent Income Any income that is infrequent and not reasonably anticipated to occur, but not more than $30 in a quarter. Income Withheld to Pay an Overpayment •Income withheld from an assistance payment, earned income, or other income source to repay a prior overpayment voluntarily or involuntarily. •Income received from any income source that is voluntarily or involuntarily returned to repay an overpayment from the same source. Exception: Count the gross income if the overpayment is excluded or due to failure to comply with regulations required under federal, state, or local public assistance programs. Income and Cash payments of a non- •The income of a non-HH member will not be considered available to County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 6 of 10 HH member the HH. In-Kind Income Exclude any gain or benefit which is not in the form of money payable directly to the HH. For example, earned and unearned in-kind, cafeteriastyle benefits, flex credits, health benefits and flexible spending accounts etc. Job Training Partnership ACT (JTPA) Earnings received from JTPA payments as follows: •All payments and earnings of a child received from participation in JTPA programs. •Payments to an adult received from participation in JTPA programs to the extent the payment reimbursements do not exceed actual expenses (for example, transportation, childcare expenses). Legally Obligated Child Support Payments •Child support payments only to the extent that they represent the HH's child support obligation, which has been ordered by a court or administrative authority. •Legally obligated child support payments: oMade to a third party (for example: a landlord or utility company) on behalf of the non-HH member in accordance with the support order. oMade by a HH with a legal obligation to obtain health insurance for a child. oPaid toward arrearages. •If the HH member obligated to pay the child support has zero income but another HH member with income is paying the child support, the child support exclusion is allowed to the CalFresh HH. •The child support exclusion is also allowed when a HH with no income pays the legally obligated child support with the CalWORKs grant. Verification: The payments must be verified. Do not allow the exclusion if the HH fails or refuses to provide the verification. Determine eligibility and allotment without the child support exclusion. Loans All loans from private individuals and commercial institutions, other than educational loans on which repayment is deferred. Military Pay The following is a list of special allowances from military pay that are excluded: •Combat Pay and Hardship Duty Pay (HDP). •Clothing Maintenance Allowance (CMA). Verification: The HH should be able to provide the deployed person’s military pay record, the Leave and Earnings Statement (LES). The LES will identify combat pay received and can be used to establish deployment to a combat zone. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 7 of 10 Non-Minor Dependent (NMD) Foster Care Income Any portion of the foster care payment that is not paid directly to the NMD. The money that is not legally obligated to be paid to the HH but is paid to a third party for a HH expense, must be excluded from income as a vendor payment. Refer to CalFresh Program Guide (CFPG) 63-223, if the extended foster care provider gives the NMD a company prepaid gift card that can be reasonably anticipated. Nonrecurring Lump-sum Payments A non-recurring lump sum received in one payment rather than recurring payments. Non-recurring lump-sum payments include but are not limited to: •Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC), Child Tax Credit (CTC), Income tax refunds, rebates, or credits. •Retroactive lump-sum Social Security, railroad retirement benefits, or other payments. •Retroactive payments for the approval of an application for any assistance program. •CalWORKs homeless assistance payments for temporary shelter or permanent housing. •Court ordered retroactive payments from any assistance program; supplemental or corrective payments received for a previous month from any assistance program. •Lump-sum insurance settlements; or refunds of security deposits on rental property or utilities. •CalWORKs Diversion payments made to divert a family from becoming dependent on if the payment is not defined as assistance. Note: Count lump sum payments as resources in the month received unless specifically excluded from consideration as a resource by other federal laws. Exclude as income and count as a resource child/spousal support disregard payments in any month. Other Public Assistance Vendor Payments CalWORKs, Refugee Cash Assistance, or Entrant Cash Assistance payment is considered an excluded vendor payment if that payment is for: •Medical assistance. •Childcare assistance. •Housing assistance payments made through a state or local housing authority. •Emergency or special assistance. •Energy assistance. Payments made under Federal Law Benefits under a state program funded under Part A of Title IV of the Social Security Act, for the purpose of energy assistance. Payments Received by Aleut Residents Payments received by Aleutian and Pribilof Islands Restitution Act. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 8 of 10 Payments under Title I of the Domestic Volunteer Services Act (AmeriCorps) Earnings of individuals (applicants and recipients) who participated in the following Title I Volunteers to America Programs payments for: oAmeriCorps*National Civilian Community Corps. oAmeriCorps*State/National. oAmeriCorps* Volunteers in Services to America (VISTA) Program payments if the person was receiving CalFresh or public assistance when the customer joined VISTA. For countable income from these programs, please refer to CFPG 63-222. Note: Temporary interruptions in CalFresh participation does not affect the exclusion once eligibility has been determined. Public Assistance Diverted to Third Parties Any payment that would normally be provided as a monetary payment to the HH that is over and above the normal grant, if the payment is made directly to a third party for a HH expense. This is considered emergency or special assistance. Radiation Exposure Compensation Trust Fund Payments received from the Radiation Exposure Compensation Trust Fund under the Radiation Exposure Compensation Act of 1990. Reimbursements These payments must be provided specifically for an identified expense, other than normal living expenses, and used for the purpose intended. Do not exclude reimbursements for normal HH living expenses such as rent or mortgage, personal clothing, or food because this would be considered a benefit to the HH. Below are examples of excludable reimbursements: •Reimbursements or flat allowances for job or training related expenses such as travel, per diem, uniforms, and transportation to and from the job or training site. •Reimbursements which are provided over and above the basic wages for these expenses are excluded. However, these expenses if not reimbursed are not otherwise deductible. •Reimbursements for the travel expenses incurred by migrant workers. •Reimbursements for out-of-pocket expenses of volunteers included in the course of their work. •Medical or dependent care reimbursements. •Reimbursements received by HHs to pay for services provided by Title XX of the Social Security Act. •Reimbursements made to the HH for expenses necessary for participation in an education component under the CFET Program. •Payments or reimbursements made under an employment, education, or training program initiated under Title IV-A of the Social Security Act after September 19, 1988, such as payments for Welfare-To-Work (WTW) supportive services. •Any allowance provided by the state or county no more frequently than annually for children’s clothes when the children enter or return to County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 9 of 10 school or daycare. Verification of attendance is not required. •Reimbursements received by HHs for participation in the Greater Avenues for Independence (GAIN) Program. Relocation Assistance Benefit Benefits paid by a public agency to a CalFresh recipient who has been relocated because of redevelopment, urban renewal, freeway construction or any other public development involving demolition or condemnation of existing housing. Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Reimbursements from the Uniform Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition Policy Act of 1970. Restitution to United States citizens of Japanese Ancestry Payments received as restitution pursuant to the Civil Liberties Act of 1988. Self-Employment Expenses Self-employment expenses. Senior Community Service Employment Program (SCSEP) Funds received by individuals aged 55 and over provided by the SCSEP under Title V of the Older Americans Act. The following organizations receive Title V funds under the Older Americans Act: •Green Thumb. •National Council on Aging. •National Council of Senior Citizen. •American Association of Retired Persons (AARP). •United States Forest Service. •National Association for Spanish-Speaking Elderly. •National Urban League. •National Council on Black Aging. Third Party Payments Payments received and used for the care and maintenance of a thirdparty beneficiary who is not a HH member. Title I of the National and Community Services Act (NCSA) Allowances, earnings, and payments made under Title I of the National and Community Service Act (NCSA) of 1990. Exclude if the participant is a dependent HH member under nineteen (19) years of age Count the earnings of the training portion of the Title I program if the participant is nineteen (19) years of age and older. The NCSA includes programs under the Serve America, American Conservation and Youth Corps and National and Community Service subtitles. Examples of programs under Title I of the NCSA include: •The Higher Education Service-Learning Program. •The AmeriCorps umbrella program, including the National Civilian County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageIncome Exclusions 63-224 10 of 10 Community Corps and the Summer for Safety programs. •Youth build programs. •The School-to-Work Opportunities Program. Vendor Payments Income not legally obligated to be paid to the HH, which are paid to a third party for a HH expense by a person or organization outside of the HH. Veterans Benefits Improvement Any amount by which the basic pay of an individual is reduced under the Veterans’ Benefits Improvement and Health-Care Authorization Act of 1986. Veterans Retraining Assistance Program Benefits earmarked by the Veterans Assistance to be used for educational or training purposes. To exclude, staff must verify that the recipient is enrolled in a qualifying institution that provides secondary, post-secondary education or the equivalent of a post-secondary diploma, or a vocational education program. Victims of Persecution Payments made to individuals because they have been determined to be victims of Nazi persecution. Wages Involuntarily Withheld by Employer Wages held by the employer as a general practice, even if in violation of law, shall not be counted as income to the HH. Workforce Investment Act (WIA) Allowances, earnings, and payments to individuals in programs under the WIA. Exclude earnings of dependent HH member under 19 years of age and under parental control of an adult HH member participating in on-thejob training under WIA. Only count the on-the-job training portion as earned income. References: ACIN I-68-17, I-41-10, I-05-08, I-18-07, I-42-07, I-01-06, I-34-04 ACL 21-137 CalFresh Letter No.358 Approved Relative Caregiver (ARC) Program Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance by 05/31/2025 Approval for Release: RICK WANNE, Director Self-Sufficiency Services

Child Support Transferred to the District Attorney Child support payments received by CalWORKs recipients, directly from a non-household member that must be transferred to the District Attorney’s office or other county agency, to maintain CalWORKs eligibility. Exclude the child support income when the customer assigns child support rights to the county (signs the Notice and Agreement for Child, Spousal and Medical Support [CW 2.1]). Contributions from People or Organizations Contributions as income when it is meant for a specific expenditure (for example, rent). Earnings of a Minor Child The earned income from a child, when they are elementary or secondary school students at least half time and have not attained their 18th birthday. •Exclude the earned income of a student turning 18 years of age during the certification period or initial application until the month following the month the student turns 18. title: 63-225 Self-Employment Income
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageSelf-Employment Income 63-225 1 of 4 Revision Date: 07/01/2022 Background: Federal law requires self-employment income to be counted as earned income in the determination of CalFresh benefits. Purpose: This section defines what self-employment income is and how it should be calculated. The section is being relocated to the income chapter. It is being revised to incorporate the language for gig-economy contractor income and merge information regarding boarders. Policy: Self-employment income is considered earned income and must be determined on a case-by-case basis. Individuals who work and receive an Internal Revenue Services (IRS) form 1099 for their earnings, or files taxes as self-employed, are considered self-employed. Staff must not restrict selfemployment to a particular type of employment or limit self-employment to how income taxes are filed. If a customer states they are self-employed, staff must consider them self-employed unless it is questionable. For example, a customer states they are an independent contractor and staff find this questionable, staff should check with the parent company to see if it considers the customer to be selfemployed or an employee. 1. Types of Self-Employment: Self-employment income shall include but is not limited to: Type Description Independent Contractor An individual who provides goods or services to another entity under a specific contract or agreement. The independent contractor is not subject to the control of the entity they are performing the services for. There is no employee/employer relationship. Gig-Economy Contractor An independent contractor paid on a per task basis for a job that is usually coordinated in conjunction with an online or application-based tool provided by a third party. Examples include, but are not limited to, UBER, Lyft, Postmates, and DoorDash. Individuals working in the gig-economy often receive payment via direct deposit. The total payment amount deposited may not reflect the gross income amount earned prior to deductions, including various fees charged by a thirdparty including application fees. Income verification, such as a paystub, physical or electronic earnings statement, or notification of per-gig gross payment, must be requested from the applicant or recipient. For tax filing purposes, gig-economy contractors will receive IRS Form 1099-MISC for total services performed for the year. Note: Healthcare subsidies paid to the gig-economy contractor must be counted in the gross income. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageSelf-Employment Income 63-225 2 of 4 Rental Property Owning a property and renting it out when a member of the household (HH) is actively engaged in the management of the property at least an average of 20 hours a week. Refer to section 63-223 on how to treat rental income if a HH member is not actively engaged in managing the property. Capital Gains The proceeds from the sale of capital goods or equipment shall be calculated in the same manner as a capital gain is calculated for federal income tax purposes. Note: If the capital gain amounts are obtained from the federal income tax forms, count the entire proceeds of the sale as gross income, even if only 50 percent of the proceeds are taxed for federal income tax purposes. Farming or Fishing Farmers and fishermen who anticipate at least $1,000 in annual gross income are entitled to offset a self-employment farming or fishing loss from other countable income. A loss occurs when the annual net self-employment income is determined to be less than zero. Deduct the loss from any other countable HH income accordingly: 1. Offset farm or fishing self-employment losses first against other selfemployment income. 2. Offset any remaining farm or fishing self-employment losses against the total amount of earned and unearned income after the earned income deduction has been applied. Roomer (Room Rental) A HH in the business of renting rooms which receives payment for the rental of rooms in the home the HH resides in. The “20 hours a week management” provision does not apply to a room rental. See Section 2 below for determining the cost of doing business for room rental. Note: When two or more HHs split the rent and all members of the HH are listed on the lease, whether one member pays a portion of the rent to the other or to the landlord directly, is a shared living situation not a roomer. Boarders (Non- Commercial) Income from boarders includes all direct payments to the HH for the boarder’s room and meals. Shelter expenses paid directly by the boarder to an individual outside the HH must not be considered income. See Section 2 below for determining the cost of doing business for a boarder and Section 63-101.8 for more information on boarders. 2. Costs of Producing Self-Employment Income: All self-employed customers are given a deduction from their gross self-employment income to cover the cost of producing the income. The customer will choose one of the following deduction types: •Actual business expenses; or •40 percent standard deduction The customer may choose the option that is most advantageous for them. Only one deduction type may be chosen at a time and will be applied to all sources of self-employment. Customers are allowed to change the method of deduction only at recertification or every 6 months. If the customer chooses actual business expenses, all expenses must be verified. If the customer states they want to use actual business expenses but does not provide verification, the deduction would be zero. If the customer does not choose a deduction type, the deduction type shall default to the 40 percent standard. The following are examples of allowable and non-allowable business expenses: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageSelf-Employment Income 63-225 3 of 4 Allowable Business Expenses Non-Allowable Expenses •Costs of goods, supplies, and materials •Livestock, seed, and fertilizer •Work-related clothing •Payments on the principal of the purchase price of income-producing real-estate, capital assets, equipment, and machinery •Business-related vehicle expenses and transportation costs incurred while on the job, including the cost of maintaining the vehicle, mileage, tolls, gasoline, insurance •Advertising costs •Postage •Cost of maintaining a job site, including a room in one’s home (allow only the portion used for business as a deduction, calculate in same manner as room rental business expense) •Telephone and electricity costs •Bookkeeping and payroll costs •Employee wages and salaries •Employee taxes •State and local sales tax paid •Professional licenses and/or permits necessary to practice a trade or profession •Insurance premiums on equipment and real estate used in producing income •Taxes on income producing property, business profit taxes, and other mandatory business-related taxes •Third-party fees •Web-based application or platform fees •Depreciation claimed for tax purposes •Net losses from previous periods •Federal, state, and local income taxes •Money set aside for retirement purposes •Personal expenses not related to the business, such as transportation to and from work, meals, clothing, entertainment, etc. •Wages, salaries, and advances paid to the business owner •Costs of maintaining a business in the individuals place of residence such as rent, utilities, and property taxes are not allowed if the client already receives these shelter and utility deductions in their CalFresh budget •Any expense that exceeds the payment a HH receives from a roomer or boarder for room rental and room and meals If a customer is self-employed as a day care provider and they choose actual business expenses, the cost of meals provided must be calculated as follows: Business Expenses Options Meals •The current reimbursement amounts used in the Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP); or •Standard amount based on estimated per-meal costs Note: If a customer reports being self-employed and having a child or adult daycare and they receive a reimbursement under CACFP please elevate to CalFresh program. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageSelf-Employment Income 63-225 4 of 4 If a customer is self-employed renting to roomers or boarders and they choose actual business expenses, the cost of doing business must be calculated as follows: Business Expenses Options Meals •The maximum CalFresh allotment for the number of boarders; or •The actual verified separate and identifiable cost of providing meals, if the actual costs are greater than the maximum monthly CalFresh allotment for the number of boarders Room •Square footage of the home; or •Number of rooms Note: Refer to Room Rental Business Expense Desk Aid for calculations. References: CFR 273.11(a), 273.11(b), MPP 63-503.41, ACIN I-03-02, I-73-04, I-37-06, I-73-09, I-84-09(e), I-31- 19. Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance by 07/31/2025 Approval for Release: Rick Wanne, Director Self-Sufficiency Services

title: 63-231 Standard and Earned Income Deductions
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Standard and Earned Income Deductions Number Page 63-231 1 of 1 Revision Date: 12/01/2023 Background: CalFresh households (HH) are entitled to various deductions when determining their net income eligibility and benefit allotment. Purpose: There has been no change in policy. This section is being updated due to sunset review. Policy: All HHs are eligible to the standard deduction. HHs with earned income are eligible to the earned income deduction in addition to the standard deduction. The standard deduction amount varies based on the HH size. Ineligible HH members will not be included in the HH size when assigning the standard deduction. For current standard deduction amounts refer to Section 63 - 1101. The earned income deduction is equal to 20 percent of the HH’s gross monthly earned income. If a HH has selfemployment income, the earned income deduction will be calculated after the allowable self-employment expenses are deducted. References: CFR 273.9(d), 273-10(e), 273.11(c) MPP 63-502.31, 63-502.13, 63-502.32 Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance on or by 12/31/2026. Approval for Release: Rick Wanne, Director Self-Sufficiency Services

title: 63-232 Medical Expenses and Deductions
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Medical Expenses and Deductions Number Page 63-232 1 of 5 Revision Date: 11/01/2024 Background: Individuals who meet the CalFresh definition of elderly and/or disabled are eligible to deduct qualifying medical expenses from their income to determine CalFresh eligibility. Purpose: This section has been updated due to the increase in the Standard Medical Deduction (SMD) from $120 to $150 and to include guidance on the treatment of reimbursable medical expenses. Information previously found in CalFresh Program Guide (CFPG) Section 63- 253 Determining Deductions for CalFresh Households is now obsolete as it has been merged into this section. Policy: An excess medical deduction is the medical expenses portion, excluding special diets, that exceeds the allowable amount per month incurred by any household (HH) member who is elderly and/or disabled. For a definition of elderly and disabled, see Section 63-101. 1. Standard Medical Deduction Elderly and/or disabled HH members who verify medical expenses within the range of $35.01 to $1 85 per month will be given a SMD of $150 per month. HHs with verified medical expenses over $185 per month may claim actual expenses in excess of $35. See table below for a summary of the SMD. Note: HH members receiving benefits as a dependent of a disabled recipient are not eligible to receive this deduction. For additional assistance, refer to the Medical Expenses and Deductions Flowchart Desk Aid. 2. Countable Medical Expenses Expenses that are not reimbursed or covered by health insurance may count as medical deductions. Countable medical expenses , including those prescribed by a licensed practitioner or other qualified professional may include but are not limited to the following: Type of Care Covered Expenses Medical • Psychotherapy and rehabilitation services. • Hearing aids and batteries. • Acupuncture, chiropractic, or herbal treatments. • Health care supplies, equipment, and incontinence supplies. • Prosthetics (including assistive devices). Verified Medical Expenses Eligibility Under $35 a month Not eligible for a medical deduction $35.01 to $185 a month HH is eligible to the SMD ($150) $185.01 a month and over Eligible to deduct actual expenses over $35 County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Medical Expenses and Deductions Number Page 63-232 2 of 5 Dental • Dentures. • Orthodontics. Eye • Eyeglasses. • Contacts. • Prescribed lens solutions. Hospitalization or Outpatient Services • Hospitalization and outpatient services must be provided by a facility authorized under state law for the following: o Treatment. o Nursing care and nursing home care. o Payments for individuals who were HH members prior to entering a hospital or nursing home. Prescription Drugs and Costs of Medical Supplies • Prescription drugs and over-the-counter medication o Excludes special diets, nutritional drinks and dietary supplements, such as vitamins. • Costs of medical supplies, sickroom equipment (including rental) or other prescribed equipment. Note: The cost of any substance considered illegal under federal law, even when prescribed, is not allowed. Health Insurance Premiums, Copays and Share of Cost (SOC) • The costs of health and hospitalization insurance policy premiums and co-pays. Note: Costs of policies that offer lump-sum payment due to death or dismemberment or income maintenance policies that offer to continue mortgage or loan payments while beneficiary is disabled are not allowable. Medicare Premiums • Medicare premiums related to coverage under Title XVIII of the Social Security Act. Maintaining Service Animals • Service and/emotional support animals must be trained to assist the individual with the medical issue for which the animal is prescribed or perform functions that elderly and/or disabled individuals cannot readily perform on their own. o Cost of securing and maintaining services animals including service animal food and veterinary bills are covered. Note: Document in the case record the reason the animal is required such as a disability and list the tasks the animal is trained to perform, no additional verifications will be required unless questionable. • Questionable information regarding service and support animals can be clarified by asking the HH only the following questions: o Is the animal required because of a disability? o What tasks is it trained to perform? County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Medical Expenses and Deductions Number Page 63-232 3 of 5 Transportation • The out-of-pocket, non-reimbursed costs of travel through a third party, such as: o P ublic transportation, taxis, or ridesharing to health care appointments and pharmacies. Note: Unless questionable, verify medical travel by personal vehicle by verbal or written statement that travel was required for medical reasons. Calculate the expense by multiplying the number of round-trip miles by the federal business standard mileage rate provided by Internal Revenue Service (IRS). Use MapQuest or Google Maps to determine mileage. Homemaker or Health Aid • Maintaining an attendant, homemaker and home health aide, or childcare services housekeeper, necessary due to age, infirmity, or illness. 3. Verification Do not limit the verification to a single type of document if the medical expense cannot be verified electronically. Assist the HH in obtaining verification if needed. For HHs to claim the excess medical deduction or the SMD, the qualifying medical expenses must be verified at application or when the expense is f irst reported. Failure to verify medical expenses must not result in denial, delay, or discontinuance of a HHs eligibility determination. 4. Billed Medical Expenses A deduction is only allowed for the portion of non -reimbursable medical expenses that the HH is responsible to pay. Any portion of the expense that is reimbursable or covered by health insurance is not an allowable expense. When an eligible HH member submits a medical bill, including hospital bills the HH’s medical expense is determined by the total amount of the non- reimbursable portion that is listed as due on the final bill (not the preliminary statement). If the eligible HH member is covered by multiple health insurance policies, a medical deduction can only be claimed after they have received or confirmed all reimbursements and payments from those insurance policies. 5. Applying the Medical Deduction Medical expense deductions are applied to the HHs budget either as a one-time deduction or averaged over the certification period, whichever the HH chooses. When a HH elects a one-time deduction, the deduction must be applied accordingly: If … then … the billing period is specified on the medical bill, a deduction will be allowed until the final day in the month the medical bill becomes due. no billing period is specified on the medical bill, the bill is considered to become due one month after the date of the bill. Note: Medical bills paid prior to the month of initial application and past due bills are not deductible. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Medical Expenses and Deductions Number Page 63-232 4 of 5 HHs reporting medical expenses during their certification period, may elect to have a one- time deduction or have the expense averaged over the remaining months of the certification period. Averaging begins in the month the change becomes effective. For HHs with 24 or 36-month certification periods, see table below. HHs with a 24 or 36-month certification period, reporting a one-time medical expense… have the option to… during the first 12 months of the certification period, • deduct the expenses for one month, or • a verage the expense over the remaining first 12 months of the certification period, or • a verage the expense over the remaining months of the certification period. after the 12th month of the certification period, • deduct the expense for one month, or • a verage the expense over the remaining months in the certification period. When an eligible HH member has a written agreement contract, or other type of plan for payment of billed medical expenses, the stipulated amount of monthly payment will be determined by the SMD. Averaging fluctuating medical expenses that are billed less often than monthly are only allowed as a deduction and averaged over the certification period if they are regularly recurring, reasonably anticipated, and verified to recur over the certification period. Previous billed expenses will only be used as an indicator that the expense is reasonably anticipated during the certification period and not to determine the average expense amount over the certification period. Fluctuating medical expenses include, but are not limited to: • Medical services and treatments received regularly, but less often than monthly. • Fluctuating monthly expenses for prescription drugs. 6. Medical Expense Reporting HHs must report and verify all medical expenses at application and recertification. The monthly medical deduction for the certification period will be determined on the reported and verified expenses, including any expected changes related to the HHs medical condition, insurance coverage and currently verified expenses. When a voluntary change in medical expenses is reported during the certification period, it must be verified under the following conditions: • For changes that increase the HHs allotment, applicable verification must be obtained, and action must be taken. The adjustment must be applied by the first benefit allotment issued, at least 10 days after the change was reported. Do not issue a supplement for a previous month or the month the medical expense is reported if benefits are adjusted timely. • For changes that result in a decrease or ineligibility, do not request verification and send the HH a No Change Notice of Action (NOA). Document the case record and follow-up at the next SAR 7 or recertification, whichever comes first. • For changes reported from sources other than the HH, do not request verification and do not take action. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Medical Expenses and Deductions Number Page 63-232 5 of 5 Example 1 Scenario A new medical expense reported and verified on April 15th would result in a benefit increase. Outcome Increase the benefit allotment beginning with the May benefit month. Do not issue a supplement for April. Example 2 Scenario A new or changed medical expense reported and verified on April 15th would result in a benefit decrease. Outcome Do not request verification. Send the HH a No-Change NOA. Document the case record for review at the next periodic report or recertification. Other Program Impacts: No Impact. References: Federal Nutrition Act (FNA) 2008 Section 17(b)(1)(A) and Section 5(5). Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 7 CFR 271.2. All County Letter (ACL) 17-35, 19-89, and 21-13, 21-101, 24-59. All County Information Notice (ACIN) I-63-05, I-06-96, and I-45-11. Manual of Policy and Procedures (MPP) 63-502.251, 63-502.3, and 63-503. Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance by 10/31/2027. Approval for Release: Rick Wanne, Director Self-Sufficiency Services

title: 63-233 Dependent Care Deduction
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageDependent Care Deduction 63-233 1 of 2 Revision Date: 01/01/2023 Background: CalFresh household’s (HH) may deduct dependent care costs from their income to determine CalFresh eligibility. Purpose: There has been no change in policy. This section is being updated due to sunset review. Policy: The dependent care deduction is the actual amount the HH pays for care for another HH member that is under the age of 18 or is of any age and incapacitated requiring care. For dependent care deductions only, incapacitation is defined as any permanent or temporary condition that prevents the individual from participating in normal activities including, but not limited to, work or school without supervision to ensure the health and safety of the individual, or a condition that makes a lack of supervision risky to the health and safety of the individual. The HH is eligible to deduct the dependent care expenses from their income if dependent care is necessary for a HH member to search for employment, accept or continue employment, comply with the CalFresh Employment and Training (CFET) requirements, attend training, or pursue education to prepare for employment. There is no cap on the amount of dependent care that may be deducted from the HH’s income. A client statement must be accepted as standard verification unless the information provided is questionable. 1. Allowable Dependent Care Expenses Dependent care expenses are only deductible if the service is provided by someone outside the CalFresh HH and the HH makes an out-of-pocket payment for the service. The following expenses are allowable as dependent care expenses: •The costs of care provided by an individual, provider, or care facility •Transportation costs to and from the care facility (standard Internal Revenue Service [IRS] mileage rate may be used) •Fees associated with activities that are necessary for the dependent to participate in the care Example: Scenario CalFresh HH consisting of mom, her 2 children ages 9 and 4. Mom and the children live with grandma but do not purchase and prepare meals with her. Mom is attending vocational school to become a medical assistant. Grandma cares for the 4-year-old (y/o) while mom is at school and mom pays grandma $400 per month. Outcome HH would be allowed a dependent care deduction of $400 per month since grandma is not part of the CalFresh HH. Note: Preschool or any other type of schooling is not considered a dependent care expense. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Number PageDependent Care Deduction 63-233 2 of 2 2. When Dependent Care Deduction is not allowed A dependent care deduction is not allowed to be claimed if another member of the CalFresh HH provides the care or when compensation for the care is provided in the form of an in-kind benefit. The dependent care deduction will not include any amount that is covered by a subsidy or paid for by another source on behalf of the HH. Example: Scenario CalFresh HH consisting of mom and 3 children ages 11, 9, and 4. Mom is attending vocational school to become a medical assistant. The 4 y/o goes to a licensed daycare center and the total cost is $1200 per month. Mom receives a $1000 monthly subsidy for the childcare. Outcome The non-reimbursed share of cost for the childcare is $200 ($1200 total cost - $1000 subsidy) therefore the HH would be allowed a dependent care deduction of $200. Example: Scenario CalFresh HH consisting of mom, her 2 children ages 9 and 4 and grandma. Mom is attending vocational school to become a medical assistant. Grandma cares for the 4 y/o while mom is at school and mom pays grandma $400 per month. Outcome A dependent care deduction would not be allowed since grandma is a member of the CalFresh HH. 3. Dependent Care Expenses that May Qualify as Medical Expenses Certain dependent care expenses may qualify as either a medical expense or dependent care expense. These expenses may be counted as either, but not counted as both. Staff must classify the expenses as medical or dependent care depending on which one is more favorable to the HH. Refer to Section 63-232 for more information on Medical Deductions. References: MPP 63-502.34, CFR 273.9(d)(4), ACL 13-102, ACL 17-98, ACL 20-135 Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance on or by 01/31/2026. Approval for Release: Rick Wanne, Director Self-Sufficiency Services

title: 63-234 Shelter Deductions and Utility Allowances for Unhoused Households
content: County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Shelter Deductions and Utility Allowances for Unhoused Households Number Page 63-234 1 of 3 Revision Date: 01/01/2026 Background: Unhoused households (HHs) who are not receiving free shelter throughout the month may be entitled to the homeless shelter deduction or may claim actual shelter expenses when determining CalFresh eligibility. Purpose: This section details the shelter expenses unhoused HHs may incur and to which deductions they may be entitled. This section is being revised to provide updated guidance to align with the policy changes regarding State Utility Assistance Subsidy (SUAS). Policy: Shelter expenses that may be incurred by an unhoused HH include but are not limited to: • Hotel and motel expenses. • Fees required to stay at a homeless shelter. • Vehicle expenses, if living in a vehicle. Note: Evaluate the shelter expenses incurred and allow the deduction that is most beneficial to the HH. 1. Homeless Shelter Deduction Unhoused HHs that do not receive free shelter for the entire month, may receive the homeless shelter deduction. Refer to Section 6 3-1101 for the current homeless shelter deduction amount. If the unhoused HH does not incur nor anticipate any shelter expenses, then they are not eligible to the homeless shelter deduction. For HHs eligible to the deduction, determine whether the HH would receive a higher benefit by applying the homeless shelter deduction or by allowing the SUAS (if the HH meets the criteria), which allows the HH to claim the Standard Utility Allowance (SUA) deduction. HHs may not receive the homeless shelter deduction and a utility allowance simultaneously. Unhoused HHs may claim actual shelter expenses instead of the homeless shelter deduction when actual expenses would entitle the HH to more benefits. When actual shelter expenses are used, the HH may also be eligible to receive the corresponding utility allowance such as SUA, Limited Utility Allowance (LUA) or Telephone Utility Allowance (TUA), if applicable. Note: The homeless shelter deduction is always deducted from the net income when determining eligibility and allotment, refer to Section 63-254 for more information. 2. Vehicle Expenses HHs living in a vehicle who are responsible for paying reasonably anticipated or reoccurring expenses on it, may claim these as a shelter expense. A vehicle expense that occurs less frequently than monthly may be averaged over the months in which it is intended to cover . Vehicle expenses include, but are not limited to: • Vehicle payments. • Collision and comprehensive insurance premiums (insurance that covers the vehicle itself). Liability and medical insurance premiums are not allowable shelter costs. • The cost of overnight parking and camping fees. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Shelter Deductions and Utility Allowances for Unhoused Households Number Page 63-234 2 of 3 • Maintenance expenses. Note: The cost of fuel, such as gasoline or diesel, to operate, heat or cool a vehicle, is not an allowable shelter or utility expense. 3. Verification Accept the shelter expenses reported by the HH verbally or on a signed application, Eligibility Status Report (SAR 7), or application for recertification without requesting additional verification. Only request verification if the shelter expenses are questionable and narrate in the case record why the information reported is questionable. If the HH is reporting vehicle insurance premiums as a vehicle expense, clarify the portion paid for collision or comprehensive coverage, since the only portion of the pr emium that is considered for shelter expense purposes is the insurance on the vehicle itself. The following examples demonstrate how to determine which deductions would be most beneficial to the unhoused HH: Example: Scenario An unhoused HH consists of husband and wife, neither is elderly or disabled (E/D). The wife receives $800 per month as a cash gift. The HH lives in their car and pays $300 per month for the car loan. They also pay $200 per month for car insurance, of which $100 of the insurance is for liability, $100 is for comprehensive coverage. The HH does not have any utility expenses. Outcome If the HH was given the homeless shelter deduction, they would be eligible to $384 per month in CalFresh benefits. If the vehicle expense of $400 per month ($300 car payment + $100 comprehensive insurance) is used as the shelter expense, the HH would be eligible to $362 per month in CalFresh benefits. In this case we would apply the homeless shelter deduction since that would be the most beneficial to the HH. The HH is not eligible to SUAS which allows the SUA deduction to be claimed due to not having an E/D HH member. Example: Scenario An unhoused HH consists of disabled mother and 10-year-old son. Mom receives $1000 per month in Social Security Disability Income (SSDI). The HH stays in a hotel 4 nights per month and pays $100 per night when staying at the hotel and pays for no utilities. Outcome If the HH was given the homeless shelter deduction, the HH would be eligible to $324 per month in CalFresh benefits. If the hotel expense of $400 per month is used as the shelter expense, the HH would be eligible to $273 per month in CalFresh benefits. If the hotel expense of $400 per month is used as the shelter expense, the HH may also claim a utility allowance. If the HH is issued the SUAS payment, it would entitle them to more benefits, making the HH eligible to $440 per month in CalFresh benefits. County of San Diego, Health and Human Services Agency (HHSA) CalFresh Program Guide Shelter Deductions and Utility Allowances for Unhoused Households Number Page 63-234 3 of 3 In this case we would use the actual shelter expense and issue the SUAS payment and allow the SUA deduction since that would be most beneficial to the HH. Example: Scenario An unhoused HH consists of single 30-year-old male. He receives $800 per month in SSDI. He lives at a homeless shelter and is responsible for paying $25 per month to stay there and pays for a telephone. Outcome If the HH is allowed the homeless shelter deduction, he is not allowed a utility allowance and would be eligible to $149 per month in CalFresh benefits. If the HH is given SUAS instead of the homeless shelter deduction, he would be eligible to $175 per month in CalFresh benefits. If the actual amount of $25 per month is claimed as the shelter expense, the HH may also claim a utility allowance. Since the HH pays for a telephone the HH is given the Telephone Utility Allowance (TUA) making him eligible to $98 per month in CalFresh benefits. If the HH is issued the SUAS payment instead of TUA, the HH would be entitled to more benefits. Therefore, if the actual amount of $25 per month is claimed as the shelter expense and the HH is issued the SUAS payment instead of TUA, he would be eligible to $183 per month in CalFresh benefits. In this case we would use the actual shelter expense and issue out SUAS allowing the SUA deduction since that would be most beneficial to the HH. References: All County Letter (ACL) 19-38, 25-68. All County Information Notice (ACIN) I-18-07, I-73-04, I-43-03, I-15-23. Manual of Policies and Procedures (MPP) 63-502.35, 63-502.36. Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) 237.9(d)(6)(i). Sunset Date: This policy will be reviewed for continuance by 12/31/2028. Approval for Release: Alberto Banuelos, Ph.D., Interim Director Self-Sufficiency Services
